source.title: SWE-Dev: Building Software Engineering Agents with Training and Inference Scaling
source.authors: Haoran Wang; Zhen-Yu Hou; Yao Wei; Jie Tang; Yu-Xiao Dong

record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream SWE-bench resolve rates across training-trajectory volumes and inference interaction budgets, a different measure and setting from language-model pretraining-loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy or sweep parameter count, pretraining tokens, and training compute. Kaplan et al. is cited as background, not tested. Rows record the study's own resolve-rate results for training-data and inference scaling.
record.test_reason: Section 5.1 scales fine-tuning trajectories for 7B and 32B agents and reports SWE-bench-Verified resolve rate rising steadily with log data size. That is a downstream-performance-versus-scale result (V6), but in a new setting: agent fine-tuning data, not pretraining scale or loss. No pretraining loss, parameter, token or compute sweep is run, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. The inference-iteration results scale test-time interaction rounds, a construct no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim the data-scaling trend is near-linear in log-log space, aligns with Kaplan et al., and is sharper for 32B. Their main framing is state-of-the-art open SWE agents (23.4% for 7B, 36.6% for 32B) built on a test-case synthesis pipeline, with RFT beating offline RL.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales SWE-agent resolve rates using training trajectories and interaction rounds rather than measuring held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size changes the data-scaling improvement; trajectory filtering retains nearly identical performance with approximately 65% of the data; iteration gains diminish at higher round counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Raising inference interaction rounds from 30 to 75 raises resolve rate: 7B 21.8% to 23.4%, 32B 34.0% to 36.6%. Gains diminish after 45 rounds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Agent task success improves with test-time interaction budget, with diminishing returns.

fits_no_version.finding: Filtering trajectories by patch similarity keeps about 65% of the data with nearly identical resolve rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning data quality can substitute for quantity in agent data scaling.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The scaling results concern SWE-bench resolve rates rather than pretraining loss. The paper gives no fitted exponents or uncertainty estimates for the scaling curves, and some plotted results lack exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-result rows omitted. Other training-method and benchmark comparisons do not measure the claim versions being tested here.

untested.parts: All: no held-out pretraining loss and no parameter, token or compute sweep.
All: no fitted law and no extrapolation to larger runs.
All: no loss power law in another regime is reported. The fine-tuning scaling uses resolve rate, not loss, and no fit is made.
Downstream performance versus pretraining scale or pretraining loss; quantitative fits or prediction; any model-size sweep beyond two fine-tuned sizes.
All: no exponents are fitted and no fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: 32B data-scaling plotted points: 28.2, 29.4, 30.6, 32.0, 34.0% across about 2^9 to 2^14 trajectories.
7B intermediate data-scaling points (e.g. 15.0, 18.0, 19.2%) and the filtered-curve values.
RFT trajectory scaling: 16.2% at 1,000 and 18.0% at 2,000 trajectories; KTO and OREO 17.2% and 17.0% at 1,800.

record.verdict_notes: The 'log-log' description conflicts with Fig. 6, whose y-axis is linear resolve rate, so the trend is log-linear. The claimed sharper 32B gain is not evident from the plotted values. Scaling here is fine-tuning data on fixed pretrained models, and no uncertainty is reported for the scaling runs. Inference scaling also changed max_tokens to 160k, which lowered the 7B result from 22.8% to 21.8%.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller pretraining runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation at fixed pretraining compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior beyond text pretraining, including other modalities and training regimes.
The study tests downstream SWE-bench resolve rates against training-data volume and inference interaction rounds, not against pretraining loss or model-parameter scale.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-7B
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of training trajectories and measured SWE-bench-Verified resolve rate.
rows.note: The paper reports this as the result at the low end of its data-scaling experiment.
rows.check: Single low-end point (574 trajectories, 13.0%). It is the baseline for r2, not an effect on its own.

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-7B
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of training trajectories and measured SWE-bench-Verified resolve rate.
rows.note: The paper says accuracy increases steadily with the logarithm of data size and describes the curve as near-linear in log-log space.
rows.check: Baseline should be r1 (13.0% at 574 trajectories), not 'not stated'. Value 22.8% at 16,639 trajectories, with a steady log-linear rise through intermediate points (Fig. 6).

source_check.correct: Baseline: 13.0% at 574 training trajectories; value: 22.8% at 16,639 trajectories, SWE-Dev-7B on SWE-bench-Verified.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, paragraph reporting the 7B scaling endpoints; Figure 6.
source_check.problem: The text explicitly provides the lower-data baseline; 'not stated' omits it.

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-32B
rows.operation_detail: Measured resolve rate while increasing training trajectories.

conditions.value: increased trajectory volume; specific plotted values not stated in text

rows.value: The 32B model shows a sharper improvement as training data increases.
rows.note: The comparison is stated qualitatively; no specific 32B trajectory-count endpoints are given in the text.
rows.check: Fig. 6 gives plotted values: 32B rises from 28.2% to 34.0% across about 2^9 to 2^14 trajectories. That is about 5.8 points, versus 9.8 points for 7B over a similar span, so the text's 'sharper improvement' is not obvious from the numbers. Record the endpoints.

source_check.problem: The qualitative comparison matches the authors' prose, but Figure 6 shows a smaller endpoint gain for 32B (28.2% to 34.0%) than for 7B (13.0% to 22.8%).

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared resolve rates with and without filtering training trajectories by patch similarity.

conditions.value: retained trajectories labeled identical or mostly identical; approximately 65% of original trajectories retained

rows.value: Nearly identical performance despite fewer training trajectories.
rows.note: No exact resolve rates for this filtered-versus-unfiltered comparison are stated in the text.
rows.check: Data-quality filtering comparison (about 65% retained, nearly identical performance). It measures neither a scaling trend nor a version's effect. Move it to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-7B
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of interaction rounds in a single evaluation episode.
rows.note: The plotted value is 21.8%; the paper states that resolve rate rises as interaction rounds increase.
rows.check: Inference-time interaction rounds are not model, data or compute scale as V6 means it. Value should be 21.8% (Fig. 7), not 'figure only'.

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-7B
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of interaction rounds in a single evaluation episode.
rows.note: The plotted value is 23.4%; the paper states that resolve rate rises as interaction rounds increase.
rows.check: Inference-iteration scaling, not a version's construct. Value 23.4% at 75 rounds (Fig. 7).

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-32B
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of interaction rounds in a single evaluation episode.
rows.note: The paper explicitly gives this result at 30 interaction rounds.
rows.check: Inference-iteration scaling, not a version's construct. This is the 30-round reference point (34.0%).

rows.subject: SWE-Dev-32B
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of interaction rounds in a single evaluation episode.
rows.note: The paper explicitly gives this result at 75 interaction rounds and describes diminishing gains at higher round counts.
rows.check: Inference-iteration scaling, not a version's construct. Value 36.6% at 75 rounds, with diminishing returns after 45 rounds.
